name: Grammar From the Class's Own Errors
title: Grammar From the Class's Own Errors
answer: Grammar From the Class's Own Errors is an approach where grammar teaching starts from anonymous mistakes that students in the class actually made. The teacher uses an AI tool to group those errors by type, then plans short lessons on the two or three most common ones. It matters because it makes grammar work specific to the class, while the book's evidence says grammar checkers by themselves add only limited improvement to writing.

crumbs.name: Reading and Writing, Kindergarten Through 12th Grade

sections.body: This idea solves the problem of grammar lessons that are generic and disconnected from what students are writing. A teacher gathers sentences from student drafts, removes names and other identifying details, and asks an AI tool to sort the errors into categories. The grouped results show which mistakes are widespread, such as comma splices or problems with subject and verb agreement. The teacher then chooses the two or three error types that matter most and builds brief lessons around them. The aim is not to cover every rule but to fix the patterns that are holding the class back.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In practice, the teacher collects anonymous sentences from student drafts and has an AI tool group the errors by type. The text describes this as a kindergarten through 12th grade approach, without separate grade band examples. The teacher reviews the groups and plans short lessons on the two or three most common errors. After a brief lesson, students practice the rule in their own writing. Students can also be asked to accept or reject grammar tool suggestions for a few sentences and explain their choices, which turns a correction tool into a learning tool.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book says the research here urges some caution. It reports a study of 119 high school students in which feedback on writing strategies combined with revision improved essays, while spelling and grammar checkers added only small gains on some measures (McCarthy et al., 2022). The text concludes that grammar matters, but it is not where most improvement in writing comes from. It also says that a brief lesson on a common error, followed by practice in the student's own writing, is usually enough.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets limits around anonymity and judgment. Identifying details must be removed before student sentences are shared or grouped. The teacher, not the AI tool, decides which errors matter most and what to teach. Students should not accept every grammar suggestion, because doing so teaches little, and they should explain why they accept or reject a few suggestions. The book also warns that grammar instruction is not the main source of writing improvement, so it should stay brief and connected to students' own writing.
